My father, born in 1948, arrived at Moscow City Clinical Hospital No. 7 on his own two feet (weighing 74.8 kg) on May 22, 2012, and left in a coffin (exhausted) on July 18, 2012. The reason for his hospitalization was a peptic ulcer, with planned surgical treatment. He was admitted to the hospital on April 28, 2012, and discharged in satisfactory condition on May 16, 2012. A planned operation - gastric resection - was scheduled for May 23, 2012. The attending physician was Dr. Y.A. Bogdasarova, MD, PhD, Professor of the 2nd Department of Hospital Surgery, I.M. Sechenov First Moscow State Medical University.

Upon admission on May 22, my father's condition was assessed as satisfactory. On May 23, a gastric resection operation was performed by Dr. Bogdasarova (or her student, it's unclear). The operation was complicated by postoperative pancreatitis, caused by a bile duct injury, which is unacceptable. This injury was discovered a day later, by which time irreversible processes threatening his life had already begun. Treatment was initiated, and my father was repeatedly transferred between the intensive care unit and the surgical ward No. 12. From May 23 to July 18, 2012, he was fed through a feeding tube and drank very little due to his condition. He experienced constant pain. During his time out of the ICU, we provided round-the-clock care. In the ICU, his condition was neglected, leading to the development of decubitus ulcers on his sacrum and a burn on his back. Our complaints to the ICU staff were dismissed, as they claimed responsibility lay with the surgeons, who were not informed. We, along with my relatives visiting my father, had to notify the surgeons ourselves. The lack of coordination between the ICU staff and surgeons was evident. There were also numerous minor shortcomings in the surgical ward No. 12 that could jeopardize a patient's health. One such issue was the attitude of the on-call doctors during their shifts: they would either sleep (and couldn't be awakened) or arrive late after being called to attend to a patient in critical condition, citing heavy workload. Weekend rounds were often infrequent, giving the impression that the illness also had a day off.

We contacted the Moscow Department of Health. Their response stated that shortcomings in patient management had led to increased toxicity. The Chief Physician of Hospital No. 7 imposed disciplinary sanctions on the staff responsible for these shortcomings in providing medical care to my father.

I was met with a barrage of abuse, I was called a spoiled woman and told I should have gone to a private clinic. A man, who was either Jewish or not Russian, was recording everything and making comments about me having two children and being afraid of anesthesia. I started crying uncontrollably. Things only got worse from there. I woke up in the ward at 12:30, feeling freezing cold in just a gown. I managed to cover myself with a blanket and looked at the time. I had been lying there half-naked for an hour and a half. A girl who had been admitted with me was brought in. She asked how I was, I mumbled something, and she told me I had been unconscious in the corridor for 10 minutes before being brought to the ward. I managed to call my husband. I felt nauseous several times and had to crawl to the sink. I felt so bad that everything was spinning. My husband came to pick me up at 5 pm, but no one had checked on me during that time. I felt like a abandoned dog. I understand that it's hard to get hold of anyone before a holiday, but anesthesia is no joke. I got up, got dressed, and wanted some tea. I went to the canteen, but the girls eating there were rude and said there were no cups, I had to bring my own. I managed to get to the elevator, a woman came and we went down together. I got dressed, went out, sat in the car, and cried from helplessness and horror at what had happened. I've never encountered such cruel treatment anywhere else. To lie there for 11 hours until 5 pm without anyone asking how I was feeling. Now I understand why people say: "If you want to die, welcome to the first hospital.

After enthusiastic online reviews of Maternity Hospital No. 20, we decided with my wife to give birth there, even for free. Being Moscow residents, we registered my wife at the women's clinic attached to the 20th maternity hospital. The doctor weighed us, listened to our pulse, and sent us for tests, which turned out to be countless. We dutifully submitted them all and waited for the birth. A month passed. My wife's due date seemed to have arrived, so we went to the maternity hospital, where we were immediately turned away by a certain "Olga Vladimirovna": there's no labor activity in you, and your tests have expired, HIV, AIDS, syphilis ended two days ago, and without them we won't take you, the hospital is "clean", we don't take pathologies. We were surprised, where was our pathology if all the tests were fine, ultrasound and CTG were in excellent condition? But the doctor was categorical, and we went to retake the tests. Getting the results, we went back to the maternity hospital, where we were again met by "Olga Vladimirovna". With obvious displeasure, she accepted our tests, but still sharply rebuked us - there are no places, sit and wait. The news that we already had 41 weeks and it was time for us to give birth was unexpected and unpleasant for her, apparently, she could no longer refuse us for some medical reasons and left us waiting in the reception room for three hours. That's when we started thinking that free births in our time are almost like an anachronism, and no one will welcome us with open arms.
My wife was eventually accepted, but sent to "pathology" because her labor hadn't started. She mentioned a "cesarean", but was strictly refused - no indications. And then it began: she lay in the ward for half a day waiting for any doctor, but no one came. Then, the next day, a catheter was inserted into her cervix, supposedly "for gel application". It's impossible to ask for a pill or injection for pain relief - you're not allowed, endure it. The next two days, the doctors played hide and seek - they appeared rarely and mostly remained silent. At night, my wife's contractions started, instead of the labor ward, she was sent to the nurse who gave her sedatives and an injection. After the continuing contractions, she was finally sent to the labor ward, placed on a chair, and they left. A drip was put in and forgotten for three hours. After persistent cries, a nurse finally came, put on a CTG, and forgot again, resulting in a meter-long cardiogram and great surprise from the doctor who came later. My wife mentioned a "cesarean" again. The answer was the same - no indications. My wife, of course, fell asleep again right there on the chair from the tranquilizers. At noon, she was woken up by surprised doctors from the next shift - let's go for a "cesarean". For this, a separate thank you to the doctor who understood that it was dangerous to delay the birth any further. That is, after three days of doing nothing to help my wife give birth, they finally took her for surgery. Everything went well - the baby was taken out, shown, and taken away. My wife was sent to the ward.
And then the most interesting part began - in the large, beautiful wards, the "paying girls" lie happily, with their own doctor attached and a nurse running at the first call. My wife has the most ordinary "Soviet" ward, a duty doctor comes occasionally, and rude nurses. Want water? Go get it yourself - after surgery! Want extra food? Wait, we'll bring a 50-gram bottle in the evening. And so on, there's milk, there's no milk - feed as you can. My wife had her first birth, she asked to be taught how to feed. The answer was - if there are problems, come as you like. On the fifth day, she was discharged with great pleasure, and it seems they were waiting for new paying patients. We, Moscow residents, find this sad and unpleasant. We can only watch as guests from the former Soviet southern republics come to give birth to their numerous offspring, and the doctors and nurses are happy to "lick" them.

Citizens, I am in shock. All the enthusiastic reviews here are either from first-time mothers or those who have nothing to compare it to. I have something to compare it to. No painkillers were prescribed (I had to prescribe them myself, ask the doctor, and then run after the nurse who was always busy to get the injection done). In three days, only one nurse, Elena Nikolaevna, remembered to treat the stitches. The pediatrician didn't even think it was necessary to come to the room and tell me about my child. I only saw the nurse (after a whole day!) who took the child, took it for an examination, and brought it back. When asked, "So, how's it going?", she replied, "Everything's fine." I'd like to ask again, "How's it going really?" A separate topic is the child whose clavicle was broken during birth, who cried constantly and didn't sleep, and only after the mother's insistence, more than a day later, the child was finally examined, the fracture was discovered, and a bandage was applied. The question is, where was the pediatrician immediately after the birth, why didn't he examine it immediately, the next morning, etc., and why does the mother have to run after everyone to make them do their job? What was particularly surprising was the presence of a child in the delivery room. A girl, the granddaughter of one of the employees, was running around the corridor, making noise, many mothers complained that they couldn't rest properly because of these cries. Excuse me, but is it allowed to have other children, besides newborns, in the delivery room? The cafeteria is something strange. I've never seen a cafeteria where it's clearly stated that meals are only served in the cafeteria. And here are the girls who, with great difficulty, come from the last births and eat standing up, instead of comfortably settling in their rooms and eating peacefully. And if the condition doesn't allow it, or the child is not sleeping at that moment, then the mother remains hungry. How awful! The food is terrible! It's just an insult to breastfeeding mothers. There's barely any meat in the diet, I only saw potatoes in the soup once in three days, instead of olive oil, there's olive margarine. Moreover, someone is constantly scolding, reprimanding you, you're always obliged to someone for something. In short, I signed a release form and left on the third day. Conclusion: This hospital is for those who are not first-time mothers, whose child is fine, and you know what to do, then the single room and staying with the child and the fact that no one bothers you (even with procedures) will please you very much.
